# Import sample files

Real export files from the logbooks pilots migrate away from, used to prove the
import templates in `internal/service/importtemplate` against whole files rather
than against header rows we wrote ourselves.

`import_samples_test.go` runs every file here through the real import pipeline —
parse, detect, map — and checks it against `manifest.json`. Nothing here is
decorative: a file that stops importing correctly fails `make test`.

## Why real files matter

A template's alias table and its header-row test are written from the same
belief about a format. If that belief is wrong, both are wrong together and the
tests still pass. Only a file the vendor's application actually produced can
settle it.

`manifest.json` records this per sample, in `provenance`:

| provenance | meaning | proves |
|---|---|---|
| `generated` | produced by this repo's own export code | authoritative; also guards backwards compatibility for exports downloaded from older versions |
| `synthetic` | hand-written from a vendor's documented column list | the template is self-consistent — **not** that it matches the real format |
| `real` | an actual, anonymised export from the application | the template works |
| `header-only` | a real export of an *empty* logbook — header row, no flights | the column names and detection; **not** the value formats |
| `real-header` | a real export's header row, with invented values, because the file itself could not be shared | detection and the column names; the value *formats* are recorded in `notes` from the real file, but only the header is in the repo |

Promoting a template from best-effort to verified means replacing its
`synthetic` sample with a `real` one and flipping `Confidence` in
`sources.go`.

## Contributing a real export

1. **Export from the application.** `manifest.json`'s `wanted` list has
   per-application instructions, and the same steps are shown in-app on the
   import screen.

2. **Anonymise it.** These files are committed to a public repository and a
   logbook is personal data. Before adding one:

   - Replace crew, instructor and PIC names with invented ones. Keep the
     *shape* — a name in `Surname, First` form must stay in that form, since
     that is exactly what the parser has to cope with.
   - Aircraft registrations may stay: they are held in public registries and
     the hyphenated forms are part of what the sample exercises. Replace one
     only if the aircraft is privately owned and identifies its owner.
   - Remove email addresses, licence numbers, employee/staff IDs, and any
     free-text remark that identifies a person or a specific incident.
   - Dates and airports can stay: they are not identifying on their own and
     they are the columns most likely to expose a format quirk.
   - Trim to 3–10 rows. Keep the *interesting* rows, not the first ones — a
     night flight, a dual flight, an instrument approach, a multi-leg route,
     anything with an empty cell where you would expect a value.

   Do not "tidy" the file otherwise. Trailing commas, a BOM, `CRLF` line
   endings, a metadata preamble, an inconsistent delimiter, a stray quote —
   those are the bugs. Keep them.

3. **Register it in `manifest.json`** with `provenance: "real"`, the template it
   must be detected as, and what its first row should produce. The tests fail on
   an unregistered file, so this step is not optional.

4. **Run `go test ./internal/api/handlers/ -run ImportSample`.** If detection
   picks the wrong template or a row does not map, that is the sample doing its
   job — fix the template in `sources.go`, not the sample.

If you cannot anonymise a file safely, do not add it. Send the **header row
alone** instead: it is what detection keys off, and it carries no flight data.

## Files here now

| File | Template | Provenance |
|---|---|---|
| `ninerlog-standard.csv` | `NINERLOG_CSV` | generated |
| `ninerlog-easa.csv` | `EASA_CSV` | generated |
| `ninerlog-faa.csv` | `FAA_CSV` | generated |
| `foreflight.csv` | `FOREFLIGHT_CSV` | synthetic |
| `flylog.csv` | `FLYLOG_CSV` | real |
| `myflightbook.csv` | `MYFLIGHTBOOK_CSV` | real |
| `logten-dynamic-export.txt` | `LOGTEN_CSV` | real |
| `wader.csv` | `WADER_CSV` | real |
| `capzlog.csv` | `CAPZLOG_CSV` | real |
| `skydemon.csv` | `SKYDEMON_CSV` | real |
| `skydemon-empty.csv` | `SKYDEMON_CSV` | header-only |
| `vereinsflieger.csv` | `VEREINSFLIEGER_CSV` | real-header |
| `vereinsflieger-extended.csv` | `VEREINSFLIEGER_EXTENDED_CSV` | real-header |

The three NinerLog files are frozen output of `writeStandardCSV`,
`writeEASACSV` and `writeFAACSV`. They are deliberately **not** regenerated by
the test suite: their job is to fail if a change to the export makes files that
older versions produced unreadable. Regenerate them only when the export format
is changed on purpose, and treat a diff in these files as a compatibility
decision rather than a formality.

The real samples are what this directory exists for. Each was written from
vendor documentation first, and every one was wrong:

- **FLYLOG.io** — wrong in every column but the date. The real export is
  `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE` with a `DURATION_*` / `TIME_*` / `NAME_*` vocabulary, so the
  file was not detected at all and 37 of its 45 columns went unmapped. It also
  carries `NAME_STUDENT=SELF`, FLYLOG's marker for the logbook owner, which the
  importer would have turned into a contact called "SELF".
- **LogTen Pro** — the Dynamic Export uses the *FAA short column names*
  (`Dual Rcvd`, `Sim Inst`, `Day Ldg`, `XC`), which are exactly `FAA_CSV`'s
  signature. LogTen files were therefore detected as FAA logbooks and imported
  as nothing: no registration, no aircraft type, no times, no crew. It also
  writes bare four-digit clock times (`1003`), which reached Postgres unparsed.
- **MyFlightbook** — carries both `Model` (a marketing description,
  "C-172 S, Cessna Skyhawk SP") and `ICAO Model` (the type code). The template
  mapped `Model`, so the aircraft type was a sentence and the fleet entry
  created to match was too. Its `Aircraft ID` is an internal numeric row ID, not
  a registration, despite being the spelling LogTen uses for exactly that. The
  file also opens with a UTF-8 BOM ahead of a quoted header, which broke the CSV
  reader's quote handling.
- **Wader** — camelCase headers (`aircraftTailnumber`, `depAirport`,
  `pilotName1`) with its own vocabulary, where the template had assumed EASA
  column names. Nothing matched, so the file was not detected and every row
  failed on four required fields at once. Wader also writes `00:00` into time
  fields that were never recorded, which derived a 777-minute block time for a
  one-hour flight — and block times override a file's own total-time column, so
  that would have inflated career totals silently.

- **Vereinsflieger** — two exports, not one, and the documented header row
  matched neither. It missed the registration (`Lfz.`), both airborne times
  (`Start`, `Landung`) and the crew column (`Begleiter/FI`), so a club export
  was detected and then failed every row on a registration the file was
  carrying all along. The extended export adds a second whole-minute duration
  that disagrees with the first — `Flugzeit` 95 airborne against
  `Blockzeit in Minuten` 112 block — and the earlier column wins a mapping tie,
  so mapping both would have logged every flight short by its taxi time. Places
  are written `Name ICAO`, the mirror image of SkyDemon's `ICAO Name`.

- **SkyDemon** — the export has *no date column and no total-time column*. A
  flight is dated by its departure timestamp and its total derived from the
  departure/arrival pair, neither of which the template had accounted for, and
  its signature matched nothing so the file was not detected. A populated
  export later showed it also writes places as "ICAO Name"
  ("EDOI Bienenfarm"), durations as whole minutes, and registrations with the
  hyphen stripped ("DEROQ" for D-EROQ).

- **capzlog.aero** — also has no date column: the flight is dated by its
  "Off Block" timestamp. "Departure"/"Arrival" are places rather than times,
  "Copi" is the co-pilot, "Remark" is singular, and the sheet carries Swiss
  mountain/glacier and rotary HESLO/HEC/HHO columns that no other logbook
  writes. The template's signature matched none of the real column names, so
  the file was not detected at all.

Seven files, eleven defects, none of which a header-row test written from the
same assumptions could have caught. Every single template written from vendor
documentation has been wrong — treat the two that remain that way
(Vereinsflieger, mccPILOTLOG) as wrong until a real file says otherwise.

Two SkyDemon samples are kept deliberately. `skydemon-empty.csv` is an export
of an empty logbook and pins the rejection message for that case;
`skydemon.csv` is populated and pins the pipeline. The empty one was supplied
first, and it could not answer the question that mattered — whether the time
columns carry a date — which is the clearest argument in this directory for
sending a file *with flights in it*.

Three products — FLYLOG.io, Wader and capzlog.aero — write a literal self-marker
into a crew cell for the logbook's owner, which is why the importer drops it
rather than creating a contact called "SELF".

Still wanted: see the `wanted` list in `manifest.json` — Vereinsflieger and
mccPILOTLOG.
